title: Independent Air 1851
summary: Independent Air Flight 1851 struck Pico Alto mountain on approach to Santa Maria Airport in the Azores on February 8, 1989. During descent, the trainee air traffic controller transmitted an incorrect QNH that was 9 hPa too high. The crew misheard due to non-standard phraseology and used the wrong altimeter setting. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and struck the mountain, killing all 144 aboard.
probable_cause: During the transmission, the trainee controller transmitted an incorrect QNH that was 9 hPa too high and used non-standard terminology. The crew did not fully hear the approach instructions and misheard the pressure setting, leading them to descend below safe altitude. The crew's failure to question the high pressure reading contributed to the accident.

factors.evidence: The trainee controller transmitted an incorrect QNH that was 9 hPa too high and used non-standard terminology at one point saying 'one octant' instead of decimal.
The crew misheard and falsely determined there were no clouds below 2,000 feet based on incorrect altitude readings.
The aircraft descended below safe altitude when they declared cleared to two thousand feet instead of the transmitted 3,000 feet.
The aircraft struck Pico Alto mountain while on approach to Santa Maria Airport.

events.text: Flight 1851 departed Bergamo Airport with communication difficulties on high frequencies
Crew contacted Santa Maria Air Traffic Control center and was handled by a trainee controller
Controller transmitted an incorrect QNH of 1027 hPa when it was actually 1018.7 hPa
The crew told the controller they were cleared to two thousand feet instead of the transmitted three thousand feet
The aircraft struck Pico Alto mountain and was destroyed with all 144 on board killed

title: Surinam Airways 764
summary: A Douglas DC-8 approaching Paramaribo initiated an ILS approach despite the ILS being unfit for operational use. The crew ignored warnings and descended below minimum altitudes without visual contact, striking trees and terrain. The captain was overage for his position and the co-pilot held false identity papers.
probable_cause: The crew descended below the minimum altitude for the approach without adequate visual references, striking rising terrain and trees.

factors.evidence: The crew descended below the minimum altitude allowed without positive visual contact with the runway.
The crew ignored audible and visual warnings and descended further despite warnings of impending crash.
First officer said I don't trust that ILS but the captain chose to use it regardless.
Final weather report stated visibility of 900 metres in fog with 400 ft cloud base.
Aircraft struck rising terrain and trees before impacting ground inverted.

events.text: Final weather report stated 900 metres visibility in fog with 400 ft cloud base.
Crew initiated ILS approach instead of cleared VOR/DME approach, though aware ILS was unfit for operational use.
No. 2 engine struck a tree at approximately 25 m above ground level, outboard right wing struck another tree shearing it off.
Aircraft rolled over and impacted the ground inverted, with 9 survivors and 178 fatalities.

notes: captain was 66 years old exceeding 60-year maximum
first officer held false identity papers

title: United Airlines 232

location.name: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa

summary: McDonnell Douglas DC-10 suffered catastrophic failure of its tail-mounted engine due to unnoticed manufacturing defect in the engine fan disk. The fan disk failure resulted in total loss of all three independent hydraulic flight control systems. The crew, with assistance from a company check pilot passenger, was able to control the aircraft using only engine thrust and land it at Sioux City. Despite the extreme difficulty of an aircraft with no hydraulic controls, the crew executed an emergency landing on a closed runway. Of 296 people on board, 111 died while 185 survived, making this crash considered a success due to superior crew resource management.
probable_cause: An undetected manufacturing defect in the number 2 engine's fan disk caused catastrophic disk failure. The failure resulted in severing all three independent hydraulic systems, creating a condition for which the aircraft was not designed. The DC-10 design assumed no single failure could cause loss of multiple hydraulic systems. The crew's exceptional resource management and decision to land at Sioux City saved the majority of occupants.

factors.evidence: Unnoticed manufacturing defect in number 2 tail-mounted engine fan disk caused catastrophic failure.
Engine rotor failure ejected high-energy fragments that severed all three independent hydraulic systems.
Total loss of all three hydraulic systems rendered conventional flight control inputs inoperative.
Crew faced extreme workload controlling aircraft with only engine thrust while troubleshooting catastrophic failure.
DC-10 design assumed no single engine failure could eliminate all hydraulic systems, assumption violated by fragment damage.
Despite total hydraulic failure, crew landed aircraft using engine thrust manipulation, saving 185 of 296 people on board.

events.text: At cruise altitude, number 2 tail-mounted engine suffers catastrophic fan disk failure due to undetected manufacturing defect.
Engine rotor failure ejects high-energy fragments that sever all three independent hydraulic systems.
Captain Al Haynes and first officer Bill Records discover total loss of hydraulic pressure and all conventional flight controls, request emergency landing.
Denny Fitch, a company check pilot on board as passenger, enters cockpit to assist with emergency procedures, having studied Japan Air Lines Flight 123 which had similar total hydraulic failure.
Crew decides to deploy landing gear using gravity fall and alternative lever system to attempt to unlock outboard ailerons that might retain some trapped hydraulic fluid.
Crew attempts to align with runway 31 using only engine thrust, executing series of mostly right-hand turns, but ends up aligned with closed runway 22 which had been closed for one year.
ATC rapidly moves fire trucks and vehicles off runway 22 after realizing aircraft will land there instead of runway 31.
Aircraft touches down on closed runway 22 and slides to stop after executing crash landing using engine thrust only, 185 of 296 people survive.

title: UTA 772 bombing
summary: UTA Flight 772 was a scheduled international passenger flight from Brazzaville to Paris. On 19 September 1989, at its cruising altitude of 35,100 feet, a suitcase bomb exploded in the forward cargo hold over the Sahara 450 km east of Agadez, causing the aircraft to break up. The explosion scattered debris over hundreds of square miles of desert. An investigation commission determined the bomb was placed in the forward cargo hold and the most plausible hypothesis was that it was inside baggage loaded at Brazzaville airport. A similar bombing had occurred five years earlier at the same airport.
probable_cause: A suitcase bomb placed in the forward cargo hold at Brazzaville airport, determined by investigation commission of the International Civil Aviation Organization.

factors.evidence: a suitcase bomb exploded in the cargo hold causing UTA Flight 772 to break up over the Sahara
Five years previously, on 10 March 1984, a bomb destroyed another UTA aircraft from Brazzaville
investigation commission could not identify who placed the bomb or which group was responsible despite earlier bombing at same airport
aircraft broke up over the Ténéré desert at 35100 ft cruising altitude

events.text: McDonnell Douglas DC-10 aircraft took off from N'Djamena International Airport on 19 September 1989 at 13:13
Aircraft proceeded normally, following routing from Moscow to Padun before crossing to Bodø Flight Information Region at FL 350, cruising at 500 km/h
Aircraft reached cruising altitude of 35100 feet over Ténéré desert, 450 km east of Agadez
Suitcase bomb exploded in the forward cargo hold at location 13-R, causing UTA Flight 772 to break up; explosion scattered debris over hundreds of square miles

title: Tan-Sahsa 414
summary: TAN-SAHSA Flight 414, a Boeing 727, crashed into Cerro de Hula mountain near Tegucigalpa, Honduras on October 21, 1989. The crew failed to follow the published step-down procedure required for the VOR/DME approach to runway 01, instead flying a continuous descent that placed them well below the published glide path. The GPWS was inoperative due to it not being required by Honduras regulation at the time.
probable_cause: The crew's failure to follow the prescribed step-down descent procedure for approach to Toncontín Airport. The aircraft descended continuously from initial approach altitude rather than executing the series of step-down fixes required in the mountainous terrain.

factors.evidence: the crew began a continuous descent from about 7600 ft MSL rather than following the prescribed step-down procedure
the aircraft's descent profile was well below the published step-down course for the entire approach
the GPWS was disconnected at the time of the accident because the system was not required by Honduras
The aircraft impacted a mountain known as Cerro de Hula at the 4800 ft MSL elevation

events.text: Tegucigalpa ATC cleared flight for VOR/DME approach to runway 01
Crew began continuous descent from about 7600 feet MSL instead of following step-down procedure
Aircraft descent profile remained well below published step-down altitude throughout approach
GPWS inoperative and unable to provide terrain warning
Aircraft struck Cerro de Hula mountain at 4800 ft MSL elevation

notes: GPWS was disconnected due to Honduras regulations
Three pilot crew members charged but case never resolved
Similar crash by SAHSA occurred 5 months later nearby
